readings.text: 1 In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. 2 He was with God in the beginning. 3 Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.
14 The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the one and only Son, who came from the Father, full of grace and truth.
15 "But what about you?" he asked. "Who do you say I am?" 16 Simon Peter answered, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God."
16 For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
15 Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

story: Last week we learned about God the Father, who loves us and makes us his children. This week we get to know the second person of the one God: Jesus, God the Son.

John starts his book with something amazing: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." "The Word" is a name for Jesus. Before there were any stars, oceans, or people, Jesus was already there with the Father. Nobody made Jesus. He has always been God, and "through him all things were made."

Then John says, "The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us." That means God the Son became a real human being. He was born as a baby, grew up, got hungry and tired, and lived with people. Jesus is fully God and fully human at the same time.
One day Jesus asked his friends, "Who do you say I am?" Peter answered, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Messiah means the Savior God promised to send. Peter was right!

Why did the Son come? Because God loves us. "For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life." Jesus came to save us from our sin, so that everyone who trusts him can live with God forever.

That is the best gift anyone has ever been given. When we give thanks, the Bible gives us the biggest thank-you of all: "Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!" Indescribable means so great that words can't fully describe it. That gift is Jesus.
weeks.enochLine: Jesus is God's Son, and he came to save me!
enochActivities: Activity: Gift box. Wrap a small box (or cover a shoebox with a blanket) and put a drawing of baby Jesus or a cross inside. Let Enoch open it and say together, "Jesus is God's best gift!"

Thank-you circle: take turns naming things to thank God for. Every time it's Enoch's turn, he ends with, "Thank you, God, for Jesus!" Paw Patrol touch: when someone needs help, the pups come running. God the Son came all the way from heaven to help and save us.
elijahQuestions: John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word." Who is the Word? Was he there before the world was made?
John 1:14 says, "The Word became flesh." What does that mean Jesus did?
When Jesus asked, "Who do you say I am?", what did Peter answer?
In John 3:16, why did God give his Son, and what does everyone who believes in him get?
jordynQuestions: John 1:1 says the Word was "with God" and the Word "was God." How does that fit with what we learned in Week 2 about one God in three persons?
Why does it matter that Jesus is both fully God and fully human? What would be missing if he were only one or the other?
People today say many things about Jesus: a good teacher, a nice man, a prophet. Why isn't "just a good teacher" enough, according to these verses?
weeks.jordynApplication: Jesus asks everyone the question he asked Peter: "Who do you say I am?" This week, think about your own answer and say it to God in prayer. At Thanksgiving dinner, or any meal this week, when it's your turn to say what you're thankful for, name Jesus and one reason why. If a friend at school or volleyball asks what you believe about Jesus, you can say, "He's God's Son, and he came to save us."
elijahAnswers: The Word is Jesus, God the Son. Yes, he was already there in the beginning, and all things were made through him (John 1:1–3).
God the Son became a real human being and lived among people (John 1:14).
"You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." (Matthew 16:16)
Because God so loved the world. Whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16).
jordynAnswers: "With God" shows the Son is a distinct person from the Father. "Was God" shows he is fully God. That is one God in three persons: the Son is not the Father, yet both are the one God.

Because he is God, he has the power to save and shows us exactly what God is like. Because he is human, he could live among us, understand what we go through, and take our place. Only someone who is both could be the Savior we need.

John says the Word was God and made all things (John 1:1–3), and Peter calls him the Messiah, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16). A teacher can give good advice, but only God the Son can save. Jesus is much more than a good teacher; he is God who came for us.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week what her answer to Jesus' question is, and listen for whether she named Jesus when the family shared what they were thankful for.
weeks.prayer: Dear God, thank you for sending your Son, Jesus. Jesus, you have always been God, and you became a person to live with us and save us. Thank you for loving us so much. Help each of us believe in you and say with Peter, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." Thank you for your indescribable gift. In Jesus' name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: Jesus is God the Son, who became a person and lived among us.
dailies.verse: The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the one and only Son, who came from the Father, full of grace and truth.
dailies.enoch: Point to yourself and say, "Jesus became a person, like me!"
dailies.elijah: What does "The Word became flesh" mean?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Jesus, God the Son, became a real human being and lived among people (John 1:14).
dailies.jordyn: John says the Son came "full of grace and truth." Why do we need both grace and truth?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Truth tells us what is right and shows us our sin. Grace is God's kindness we don't deserve. Jesus brings both: he tells us the truth, and he forgives and helps us.
dailies.action: Read John 1:14 together, then each person names one thing Jesus did when he lived on earth, like healing people, teaching, or welcoming children.
dailies.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for becoming one of us and living among us. Thank you for showing us what the Father is like, full of grace and truth. Help us know you better and show your grace and truth to others. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: John begins his Gospel by calling Jesus "the Word," who was with God in the beginning and was God. In verse 14 something amazing happens: the Word became flesh, a real human who lived among people. John and the other disciples saw his glory, full of grace and truth. Verse 18 says no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is himself God, has made him known. That is our big idea: Jesus has always been God, and he became a person to save us and show us what God is like. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Wrap a doll or stuffed animal in a blanket like a baby and say, "God the Son became a baby: Jesus!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 18, who has made God known to us? Why do we need someone to show us what God is like?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The one and only Son, who is himself God (verse 18), which means Jesus. We need him because no one has ever seen God (verse 18); Jesus shows us God's love, power, and goodness.
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 17 says grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Think of a story about Jesus you know: what does it show you about what God is like? How could you show both grace and truth to someone this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Any true example: welcoming children shows God loves the little and overlooked; healing shows his power and compassion; forgiving shows his grace. For the second part, anything that is honest and kind together, like telling the truth gently or forgiving a teammate.
dailies.passageText: 14 The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us. We have seen his glory, the glory of the one and only Son, who came from the Father, full of grace and truth. 15 (John testified concerning him. He cried out, saying, “This is the one I spoke about when I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me because he was before me.’”) 16 Out of his fullness we have all received grace in place of grace already given. 17 For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. 18 No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is himself God and is in closest relationship with the Father, has made him known.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: Peter knew who Jesus is: the Messiah, the Son of the living God.
dailies.verse: 15 "But what about you?" he asked. "Who do you say I am?" 16 Simon Peter answered, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God."
dailies.enoch: A parent asks, "Who is Jesus?" Enoch answers, "God's Son!"
dailies.elijah: What did Peter say when Jesus asked, "Who do you say I am?"
dailies.elijahAnswer: "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God." (Matthew 16:16)
dailies.jordyn: Jesus didn't just ask what other people thought; he asked, "Who do you say I am?" Why does everyone have to answer that for themselves?
dailies.jordynAnswer: No one can believe for us. Parents and church can teach us, but each person has to trust Jesus for themselves. John 3:16 says "whoever believes."
dailies.action: Go around the table and have each person finish the sentence "Jesus is..." with something true from this week.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for showing us who Jesus is. Jesus, we believe you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Help each of us answer your question for ourselves, and help us tell our friends who you are. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus took his disciples to a place called Caesarea Philippi, far to the north, and asked what people were saying about him. People had lots of guesses: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or another prophet. Then Jesus made it personal: "But what about you? Who do you say I am?" Peter answered, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God," and Jesus said the Father in heaven had shown him that. Messiah means the promised King God sent to save his people, and Son of the living God means Jesus is God the Son, just like our big idea says. Lots of people today still have opinions about Jesus, but the question that matters is what you believe about him.
dailies.enochActivity: Play a question game: a parent asks, "Who made the stars?" (God!) "Who loves me?" (Jesus!) "Who is God's Son?" (Jesus!) Give Enoch a high five for each answer.
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 14, what were people guessing about who Jesus was? (Listen for a name you know!) Why do you think Jesus asked the disciples for their own answer?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Some said John the Baptist, others said Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets (verse 14). Jesus wanted each disciple to know and say for himself who Jesus really is (verse 15).
dailies.jordyn2: In verse 17, Jesus says Peter didn't learn this from "flesh and blood"; the Father revealed it. What does that tell you about how people come to believe in Jesus? If a friend asked, "Who is Jesus?" what would you say?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Believing in Jesus is a gift God gives; the Father opens our eyes (verse 17). That's why we pray for our friends, not just argue with them. Any true answer works for the second part, such as: Jesus is the Son of God who came to save us.
dailies.passageText: 13 When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” 14 They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” 15 “But what about you?” he asked. “Who do you say I am?” 16 Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.” 17 Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by my Father in heaven.

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: Jesus showed he is God by calming the storm.
dailies.verse: 39 He got up, rebuked the wind and said to the waves, "Quiet! Be still!" Then the wind died down and it was completely calm. 40 He said to his disciples, "Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?" 41 They were terrified and asked each other, "Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!"
dailies.enoch: Make storm noises (whoosh!), then say, "Quiet! Be still!" and everyone freezes.
dailies.elijah: What happened when Jesus said, "Quiet! Be still!"?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The wind died down and it was completely calm (Mark 4:39).
dailies.jordyn: The disciples asked, "Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!" How would you answer their question using what we learned this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He is God the Son, the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3). The wind and the waves obey him because he made them.
dailies.action: Storm game: everyone makes wind and wave sounds and rocks like a boat. When the leader says, "Quiet! Be still!", everyone freezes. Take turns being the leader.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, you are stronger than any storm, and even the wind and the waves obey you. When we feel scared, help us remember that you care. Teach us to trust you instead of being afraid. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: After a long day of teaching by the lake, Jesus and his disciples got into a boat to cross over to the other side. A furious storm came up, and waves broke over the boat until it was nearly swamped, but Jesus was asleep on a cushion. The scared disciples woke him, and he simply spoke to the wind and waves, "Quiet! Be still!" and it was completely calm. Only the One who made the wind and the waves can command them, which is why the disciples asked, "Who is this?" Our big idea answers them: Jesus is God the Son. Our storms might be a scary night, a hard test, or a big worry, and Jesus is just as strong in those as he was on the lake.
dailies.enochActivity: With a grown-up, make waves in a bowl of water or the bathtub with your hand. Then say, "Quiet! Be still!" and hold your hand still while the water calms down.
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 38, what was Jesus doing when the storm came? Why could Jesus sleep while everyone else was scared?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion (verse 38). He wasn't afraid because he is God the Son; even the wind and the waves obey him (verse 41).
dailies.jordyn2: In verse 38 the disciples asked, "Teacher, don't you care if we drown?" Have you ever felt like God didn't care? What does the rest of the story show about Jesus, and what is a "storm" in your life you can bring to him?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Jesus did care: he got up, calmed the storm, and then helped them grow in faith (verses 39–40). Feeling scared doesn't mean God has stopped caring. Any honest answer works for her storm; pray about it together.
dailies.passageText: 35 That day when evening came, he said to his disciples, “Let us go over to the other side.” 36 Leaving the crowd behind, they took him along, just as he was, in the boat. There were also other boats with him. 37 A furious squall came up, and the waves broke over the boat, so that it was nearly swamped. 38 Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion. The disciples woke him and said to him, “Teacher, don’t you care if we drown?” 39 He got up, rebuked the wind and said to the waves, “Quiet! Be still!” Then the wind died down and it was completely calm. 40 He said to his disciples, “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?” 41 They were terrified and asked each other, “Who is this? Even the wind and the waves obey him!”

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: God gave his Son because he loves the world.
dailies.verse: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
dailies.enoch: Spread your arms wide and say, "God loves me THIS much!"
dailies.elijah: In John 3:16, who does God love, and what did he give?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God loves the world, and he gave his one and only Son (John 3:16).
dailies.jordyn: John 3:16 says "whoever believes." What does that tell you about who can be saved?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Anyone. It doesn't depend on where you come from or how good you are. Whoever believes in Jesus has eternal life.
dailies.action: Read John 3:16 together, putting each family member's name in place of "the world": "For God so loved Elijah..."
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for loving the world so much that you gave your one and only Son. Thank you, Jesus, for coming to save us, not to condemn us. Help us believe in you and share this good news. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus said these words to a man named Nicodemus, a religious leader who came to talk with him at night. Jesus explained why he came: God loved the world so much that he gave his one and only Son. Verse 17 says God didn't send his Son to condemn the world, which means to declare it guilty, but to save it. Whoever believes in him is not condemned and has eternal life. This is the heart of our big idea: Jesus is God the Son, who became a person to save us because God loves us. Think of a rescue team on a mountain: they don't come to blame the hikers who are stuck; they come to carry them home.
dailies.enochActivity: Make a gift: wrap a small toy in a napkin or paper, give it to someone, and say, "God gave us Jesus because he loves us!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 17, why did God send his Son into the world? Why is that good news for us?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: To save the world through him, not to condemn it (verse 17). It's good news because we all do wrong, and Jesus came to rescue us.
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 18 says whoever does not believe "stands condemned already." Why does believing in Jesus make all the difference? Who is someone you could pray for this week who doesn't know Jesus yet?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Because of sin, everyone already stands guilty; Jesus is the rescue God gave, so whoever believes in him is not condemned (verses 16–18). Any real name works for the second part.
dailies.passageText: 16 For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him. 18 Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe stands condemned already because they have not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: Jesus is God's best gift, so we give thanks.
dailies.verse: Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!
dailies.enoch: Say, "Thank you, God, for Jesus!"
dailies.elijah: What does "indescribable" mean, and what is God's indescribable gift?
dailies.elijahAnswer: It means too great for words to fully describe. God's gift is Jesus, his Son (2 Corinthians 9:15; John 3:16).
dailies.jordyn: Why should thanking God for Jesus come first, before food, family, and other good things?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Every good gift comes from the Father (James 1:17), but Jesus is the greatest gift, because through him we are forgiven and become God's children forever. The other gifts are good; Jesus is best.
dailies.action: Thankful challenge: at a meal today, each person names three things they're thankful for, and the last one is always Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Thank you, God, for your indescribable gift, Jesus. Thank you for every good thing you give us. Make us generous, so that others will thank you too. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul wrote this letter to the church in Corinth while they were collecting a gift to help needy Christians. He says their generous giving does two things: it meets real needs, and it makes people overflow with thanks to God. Then Paul bursts out in praise: "Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!" Every gift we give or receive points back to God's greatest gift, Jesus, who is too wonderful for words. That is our big idea: Jesus is God's best gift, so we give thanks for him. When you get a gift that is just right, you can't stop saying thank you, and Jesus is the gift that keeps us thankful forever.
dailies.enochActivity: Color a gift box on paper, and with a grown-up's help draw a cross or write "Jesus" inside it. Show the family and say, "Jesus is God's best gift!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 12, the Corinthians' giving overflows in many expressions of what? Why does giving to others make people thankful to God?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Thanks to God (verse 12). When people are helped, they see God taking care of them through his people, so they praise God (verses 12–13).
dailies.jordyn2: Paul calls Jesus an "indescribable gift." Try anyway: in one sentence, why is Jesus the best gift? How could you be generous to someone this week, the way the Corinthians were?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Any true sentence, such as: through Jesus we are forgiven and become God's children forever (John 1:12; John 3:16). Any real idea works for the second part: sharing, helping a teammate, or giving time or a gift.
dailies.passageText: 12 This service that you perform is not only supplying the needs of the Lord’s people but is also overflowing in many expressions of thanks to God. 13 Because of the service by which you have proved yourselves, others will praise God for the obedience that accompanies your confession of the gospel of Christ, and for your generosity in sharing with them and with everyone else. 14 And in their prayers for you their hearts will go out to you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you. 15 Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: Jesus is God the Son. He has always been God, he became a person, and he came to save us.
dailies.verse: But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
dailies.enoch: Ask, "Who is Jesus?" (God's Son!) "Why did he come?" (To save me!)
dailies.elijah: Name two things we learned about Jesus this week.
dailies.elijahAnswer: Any two: he was there in the beginning and made all things; he became a person; Peter called him the Messiah, the Son of the living God; he calmed the storm; God gave him because he loves the world; he is God's indescribable gift.
dailies.jordyn: John says he wrote his book "that you may believe." What is one thing from this week that helps you believe Jesus is the Son of God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Any answer from the week: he was with God and was God from the beginning (John 1:1), the wind and waves obeyed him (Mark 4:39–41), Peter confessed him as the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16), and God gave him out of love (John 3:16).
dailies.action: Read John 20:31 together, then each person shares one thing they learned about Jesus this week. Next lesson: God promises a Savior.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, you are our Lord and our God. Thank you for rising from the dead and for the Bible that helps us believe. When we have doubts, help us trust you like Thomas did. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week on Jesus the Son. After Jesus rose from the dead, his disciple Thomas said he would not believe unless he saw and touched Jesus' wounds. A week later Jesus came and stood among the disciples even though the doors were locked, showed Thomas his hands and side, and said, "Stop doubting and believe." Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God!" John says he wrote his book so that we would believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life in his name. This week we learned that Jesus was there in the beginning, became a person, calmed the storm, and was given because God loves the world, and Jesus says those who believe without seeing are blessed.
dailies.enochActivity: Hold out your hands the way Jesus showed Thomas, then point up and say, "Jesus is my Lord and my God!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 28, what did Thomas call Jesus? Why is that a big deal?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: "My Lord and my God!" (verse 28). It's a big deal because Thomas said out loud that Jesus is God, and Jesus did not correct him.
dailies.jordyn2: In verse 29 Jesus says, "blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." That includes us. Why can we believe even though we haven't seen Jesus? When is it hardest for you to trust what you can't see?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God gave us the eyewitness record, written "that you may believe" (verses 30–31). Any honest answer works for the second part.
dailies.passageText: 26 A week later his disciples were in the house again, and Thomas was with them. Though the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you!” 27 Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.” 28 Thomas said to him, “My Lord and my God!” 29 Then Jesus told him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” 30 Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not recorded in this book. 31 But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

weeks.bigIdea: Long before Jesus was born, God promised to send a Savior, and God always keeps his promises.

howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

readings.text: 2 The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of deep darkness a light has dawned.

6 For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders. And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. 7 Of the greatness of his government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on David's throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever. The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this.
2 "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times."
4 But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.

story: Last week we learned that Jesus is God the Son, who became a person to save us. Now Advent begins. Advent means "coming." It is a time to remember how God's people waited for the Savior to come, and to get our hearts ready to celebrate his birth at Christmas.

When people turned away from God, sin made the world a dark and sad place. But God did not leave his people without hope. Hundreds of years before Jesus was born, God gave promises through his prophets, messengers who spoke God's words.
The prophet Isaiah said, "The people walking in darkness have seen a great light." Sin makes life dark, like a room with no lights on. God promised to send a light into the darkness.

Isaiah also said, "For to us a child is born, to us a son is given." This child would have amazing names: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. He would be a King from David's family, and his kingdom would never end. Who could be born as a baby and also be called Mighty God? Only Jesus, God the Son!
Another prophet, Micah, even told where this ruler would be born: Bethlehem, a small town. God chose a little place for his great King.

God's people waited a long, long time. But God never forgets his promises. The Bible says, "When the set time had fully come, God sent his Son." Right on God's schedule, Jesus was born in Bethlehem, just as God said. And he came so that we could become God's children, just like we learned in Week 3.
weeks.enochLine: God promised a Savior, and God always keeps his promises!
enochActivities: Activity: Light in the dark. Turn off the lights and sit together in the dark for a moment. Then turn on a flashlight and say together, "Jesus is the light God promised!"

Promise game: a parent makes a small promise ("After we read, I'll give you a big hug") and keeps it right away. Say together, "God keeps his promises too!" Paw Patrol touch: the pups can count on Ryder to show up, but God is even more faithful. He has never broken a single promise.
elijahQuestions: In Isaiah 9:2, what did the people walking in darkness see?
Isaiah 9:6 gives the promised child four names. Can you name them?
According to Micah 5:2, in what town would the ruler be born?
Galatians 4:4 says God sent his Son "when the set time had fully come." Did God forget his promise while people waited?
jordynQuestions: Isaiah says "a child is born" and calls him "Mighty God." How does that fit with what we learned last week about Jesus?
Isaiah also calls him "Everlasting Father," but Jesus is the Son, not the Father. What do you think this name tells us about the kind of King he is?
God's people waited hundreds of years for the Savior. What does that teach us about trusting God when we have to wait?
weeks.jordynApplication: Waiting is hard: waiting for a volleyball tournament, a test grade, Christmas, or an answer to prayer. This week, write down one thing you're waiting for and pray about it each day. When you feel impatient, remember that God's people waited a long time for the Savior, and God kept his promise right on time. Then look for one way to bring a little light to someone at school, like including someone who is left out.
elijahAnswers: A great light (Isaiah 9:2).
Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6).
Bethlehem (Micah 5:2).
No. God sent Jesus right at the time he planned (Galatians 4:4). God always keeps his promises.
jordynAnswers: A child would be born, so he would be fully human, and he would be Mighty God, so he would be fully God. That is exactly who Jesus is: God the Son, who became a person (John 1:1, 14).

It describes how this King cares for his people: forever, the way a loving father protects and provides. It does not mean the Son and the Father are the same person. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are still three persons and one God.

God's timing is perfect even when it feels slow. He was working the whole time and kept his word right on time (Galatians 4:4). We can wait with hope because God does not lie or forget his promises (Numbers 23:19).
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week what she's waiting for and how she's been praying about it, and notice any kindness she shows to someone at school.
weeks.prayer: Dear God, thank you for promising a Savior long ago and for keeping your promise by sending Jesus. Thank you that Jesus is the light in the darkness, the Mighty God, and the Prince of Peace. Help us trust you while we wait, because you always keep your promises. As we get ready for Christmas, help our hearts get ready for Jesus. In Jesus' name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: God promised a child who would be called Mighty God and Prince of Peace.
dailies.verse: For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders. And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
dailies.enoch: Hold up four fingers and say the names with a parent: "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace!"
dailies.elijah: Which name for the promised child is your favorite, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Any of the four with a reason: Wonderful Counselor (he gives perfect wisdom), Mighty God (he is God), Everlasting Father (he cares for his people forever), Prince of Peace (he brings peace with God).
dailies.jordyn: "To us a son is given" sounds like John 3:16 from last week. How are the two verses connected?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Isaiah promised that a son would be given. John 3:16 says God gave his one and only Son. Jesus is the Son God promised and then gave.
dailies.action: Read Isaiah 9:6 together, then each person picks one name and says what it tells us about Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Lord Almighty, thank you for promising a child who is Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Thank you for sending Jesus to keep that promise. Help us trust him as our King this Advent. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Isaiah was a prophet who lived about 700 years before Jesus was born, at a time when God's people were afraid of enemy armies. God gave Isaiah a promise: the darkness would end, the enemy's heavy yoke would be broken, and a child would be born, a son given, who would rule forever. His names tell us who he is: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Verse 7 says he will reign on David's throne with justice and righteousness forever, and the LORD himself will make it happen. That is our big idea: long before Jesus was born, God promised a Savior, and God always keeps his promises. Advent means "coming," and it's when we remember God's people waiting for this promised child.
dailies.enochActivity: Count four fingers for the four names. For "Prince of Peace," put on a pretend crown, then sit very still and quiet for five seconds: peace!
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 7, how long will his government and peace last? Why does that matter?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: There will be no end; he will reign from that time on and forever (verse 7). It matters because every other king grows old or loses power, but Jesus will rule forever.
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 7 ends, "The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this." Who makes the promise come true, and why is that comforting? Which of the four names do you need most this week, and why?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The LORD himself; his zeal, meaning his passionate commitment, guarantees it, so it doesn't depend on people (verse 7). Any of the four names with a real reason works for the second part.
dailies.passageText: 2 The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of deep darkness a light has dawned. 3 You have enlarged the nation and increased their joy; they rejoice before you as people rejoice at the harvest, as warriors rejoice when dividing the plunder. 4 For as in the day of Midian’s defeat, you have shattered the yoke that burdens them, the bar across their shoulders, the rod of their oppressor. 5 Every warrior’s boot used in battle and every garment rolled in blood will be destined for burning, will be fuel for the fire. 6 For to us a child is born, to us a son is given, and the government will be on his shoulders. And he will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. 7 Of the greatness of his government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on David’s throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever. The zeal of the LORD Almighty will accomplish this.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: Jesus is the great light God promised for a dark world.
dailies.verse: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of deep darkness a light has dawned.
dailies.enoch: Turn off the light, then flip it back on and shout, "A great light!"
dailies.elijah: What did the people walking in darkness see?
dailies.elijahAnswer: A great light (Isaiah 9:2).
dailies.jordyn: Isaiah uses darkness as a picture. What kind of darkness was he talking about, and how does Jesus bring light?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Not just nighttime, but the darkness of sin, sadness, and being far from God. Jesus brings light by showing us what God is like, forgiving our sin, and bringing us back to God.
dailies.action: Flashlight game: turn the lights down. One person hides a Bible in the room, and the others use a flashlight to find it. Whoever finds it reads Isaiah 9:2 out loud.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, thank you for being the great light God promised. Thank you for shining into our darkness and bringing us to God. Help us shine your light at school, on our teams, and at home. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Yesterday we read Isaiah's promise that people walking in darkness would see a great light. Hundreds of years later, Jesus grew up, began his ministry, and moved to the town of Capernaum by the lake in Galilee. Matthew says this happened to fulfill what Isaiah said: in that very region, the people living in darkness saw a great light. Jesus is that light, and God kept his promise, just as our big idea says. The darkness Isaiah meant is not only nighttime, but sin, sadness, and being far from God. A flashlight makes a dark room feel safe because you can see where you're going, and Jesus shows us the way to God.
dailies.enochActivity: With a grown-up, shine a flashlight on each person in the family while you say, "Jesus is the light!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 13, what town did Jesus go and live in? Why does Matthew say Jesus went there?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Capernaum, by the lake (verse 13). Matthew says it was to fulfill what was said through the prophet Isaiah (verse 14), so the promise of a great light would come true.
dailies.jordyn2: Isaiah made this promise hundreds of years before Jesus, and Matthew shows it came true in the same region. What does that tell you about God's Word? Where in your life (school, team, friends) is Jesus' light needed, and how could you shine it?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God's Word is true and reliable; what he says, he does, even centuries later (verses 14–16). Any real place and idea works for the second part.
dailies.passageText: 12 When Jesus heard that John had been put in prison, he withdrew to Galilee. 13 Leaving Nazareth, he went and lived in Capernaum, which was by the lake in the area of Zebulun and Naphtali— 14 to fulfill what was said through the prophet Isaiah: 15 “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles— 16 the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death a light has dawned.”

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: God told ahead of time where the Savior would be born.
dailies.verse: "But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times."
dailies.enoch: Say "Bethlehem!" and clap once for each part: Beth-le-hem.
dailies.elijah: What town did Micah say the ruler would come from?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Bethlehem (Micah 5:2).
dailies.jordyn: Micah says Bethlehem was "small among the clans of Judah," and the ruler's "origins are from of old, from ancient times." What do those two details tell you?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God often uses small, overlooked places and people for his big plans. And a ruler whose origins are from ancient times points to Jesus, who was alive before he was born, because he has always been God (John 1:1).
dailies.action: Find Bethlehem on a Bible map or an online map together, then read Micah 5:2.
dailies.prayer: Lord, thank you for choosing little Bethlehem and for keeping your promise exactly as you said. Jesus, thank you for being our Shepherd who keeps us safe. Help us notice and care for people who feel small. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Micah was a prophet who lived around the same time as Isaiah. God told him the exact town the promised ruler would come from: Bethlehem, a small, ordinary village in Judah. This ruler's origins are "from of old, from ancient times," which points to Jesus, who lived before he was born because he is God the Son. Verse 4 says he will shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, his people will live securely, and his greatness will reach to the ends of the earth. About 700 years later, Jesus was born in Bethlehem, just as God said. It's like a train schedule that names the exact station: God's promises arrive right where he says they will.
dailies.enochActivity: Pretend to be a shepherd: use a wooden spoon as a staff, gather stuffed-animal "sheep" into a pile, and say, "Jesus takes care of his sheep!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 4, what will the ruler do for his flock? Why is a shepherd a good picture of Jesus?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD (verse 4). A shepherd leads, feeds, and protects his sheep, and Jesus does that for his people, so they live securely (verse 4).
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 4 says his people "will live securely." What do people usually look to for security, and how is being safe with Jesus different? How could you include someone who feels small or overlooked this week, the way God chose little Bethlehem?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: People look for security in friends, grades, looks, or being good at a sport, but those can change. Jesus shepherds in the strength of the LORD, so his people are truly secure (verse 4). Any real idea works for the second part.
dailies.passageText: 2 “But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times.” 3 Therefore Israel will be abandoned until the time when she who is in labor bears a son, and the rest of his brothers return to join the Israelites. 4 He will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. And they will live securely, for then his greatness will reach to the ends of the earth.

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: God always keeps his promises.
dailies.verse: God is not human, that he should lie, not a human being, that he should change his mind. Does he speak and then not act? Does he promise and not fulfill?
dailies.enoch: Ask, "Does God keep his promises?" (Yes!)
dailies.elijah: According to Numbers 23:19, does God ever lie or fail to do what he promised?
dailies.elijahAnswer: No. God is not human, that he should lie. He does what he says and keeps every promise (Numbers 23:19).
dailies.jordyn: People sometimes break promises, even when they mean well. Why can we trust God's promises in a way we can't trust anyone else's?
dailies.jordynAnswer: People can forget, change their minds, or be unable to do what they said. God never lies, never changes his mind, and is powerful enough to do everything he says (Numbers 23:19).
dailies.action: Promise challenge: each person makes one small promise to someone in the family today and keeps it. At bedtime, thank God that he always keeps his promises.
dailies.prayer: God, thank you that you never lie and never change your mind. Every promise you make, you keep. Help us trust your promises and be people who keep our word too. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Long ago, while God's people traveled through the wilderness, a king named Balak was afraid of them. He sent for a man named Balaam to curse Israel, but God would only let Balaam speak blessings. In this passage Balaam tells the king the truth: God is not like people. He doesn't lie or change his mind; when he speaks, he acts, and when he promises, he fulfills. Verse 20 says God has blessed, and no one can change it. That is why we can trust the promise of a Savior we're learning about this week: God always keeps his promises. A friend might promise to save you a seat and forget, but God never forgets a promise.
dailies.enochActivity: Promise game: a parent makes Enoch a tiny promise, like "I'll give you a hug in one minute," and keeps it. Then say together, "God always keeps his promises!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 20, what command did Balaam receive? Why couldn't Balaam change it?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: A command to bless (verse 20). He couldn't change it because God had blessed, and no one can undo what God has decided (verse 20).
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 19 asks, "Does he speak and then not act? Does he promise and not fulfill?" Name one promise from this week and show how God kept it. How can you be someone whose word can be trusted?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Examples: God promised a son would be given to rule forever (Isaiah 9:6) and sent Jesus; he promised a great light (Isaiah 9:2), and Jesus brought it (Matthew 4:16); he promised a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and Jesus was born there. For the second part: keep small promises, tell the truth, and follow through.
dailies.passageText: 18 Then he spoke his message: “Arise, Balak, and listen; hear me, son of Zippor. 19 God is not human, that he should lie, not a human being, that he should change his mind. Does he speak and then not act? Does he promise and not fulfill? 20 I have received a command to bless; he has blessed, and I cannot change it.

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: God is patient, and we can trust him while we wait.
dailies.verse: The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say, "Thank you, God, for being patient with me."
dailies.elijah: Is the Lord slow in keeping his promise?
dailies.elijahAnswer: No. The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise; he is patient (2 Peter 3:9).
dailies.jordyn: Peter wrote this about waiting for Jesus to come back. He says God's waiting is really patience, because he wants everyone to come to repentance. How does that change the way you see waiting?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God's waiting isn't forgetting; it's mercy. He is giving more people time to turn to him. That makes us thankful, and eager to tell others about Jesus.
dailies.action: Pray together for one person you know who doesn't know Jesus yet, asking God to bring them to himself.
dailies.prayer: Lord, thank you for being patient with us and for keeping your promises at just the right time. Like Simeon, help us wait for you with faith and joy. Please bring the people we love to know Jesus. In his name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Simeon was an old man in Jerusalem who loved God and was waiting for the promised Savior. The Holy Spirit had shown him that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Messiah. Simeon waited, and God kept his word: when Mary and Joseph brought baby Jesus to the temple, Simeon took him in his arms and praised God, saying, "My eyes have seen your salvation." Our key verse says the Lord is not slow in keeping his promise; he is patient, because he wants everyone to come to him. God's people waited hundreds of years for Jesus to come, and now we wait for him to come back, trusting that God's timing is always right. Waiting for Christmas morning can feel slow, but it always comes, and God's promises are even more certain.
dailies.enochActivity: Practice waiting: a parent hides a small treat in one hand, and Enoch counts slowly to ten before opening it. Then say, "God's promises are worth waiting for!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 28, what did Simeon do when he saw baby Jesus? Why was he so happy?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He took Jesus in his arms and praised God (verse 28). He was happy because God had kept his promise: Simeon's eyes had seen God's salvation (verses 26 and 30).
dailies.jordyn2: Simeon waited a long time, and verse 25 says he stayed righteous and devout. What helps someone keep trusting God while they wait? What are you waiting on God for right now?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Holding on to God's promise and staying close to him: the Holy Spirit was on Simeon, and he went to the temple when the Spirit moved him (verses 25–27). Any honest answer works for the second part; pray about it together.
dailies.passageText: 25 Now there was a man in Jerusalem called Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was on him. 26 It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah. 27 Moved by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. When the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what the custom of the Law required, 28 Simeon took him in his arms and praised God, saying: 29 “Sovereign Lord, as you have promised, you may now dismiss your servant in peace. 30 For my eyes have seen your salvation, 31 which you have prepared in the sight of all nations: 32 a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel.”

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: God promised a Savior long ago, and he kept his promise by sending Jesus.
dailies.verse: 4 But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.
dailies.enoch: Ask, "What did God promise?" (A Savior!) "Who is the Savior?" (Jesus!)
dailies.elijah: Name two promises about the Savior we learned this week.
dailies.elijahAnswer: Any two: he would be a great light (Isaiah 9:2); he would be called Mighty God and Prince of Peace and reign forever (Isaiah 9:6–7); he would be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2); God would send him at just the right time (Galatians 4:4).
dailies.jordyn: Galatians 4:5 says Jesus came "that we might receive adoption to sonship." How does that connect to what we learned about God the Father in Week 3?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Adoption means being brought into a family. In Week 3 we learned that everyone who receives Jesus becomes a child of God (John 1:12). Jesus came so we could belong to the Father's family.
dailies.action: Read Galatians 4:4–5 together, then each person shares one thing they learned about God's promises this week. Next lesson: the angel visits Mary.
dailies.prayer: Abba, Father, thank you for sending your Son right on time and for sending your Spirit into our hearts. Thank you that we are not slaves, but your children. Help us wait for Christmas with thankful hearts. In Jesus' name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our Advent week. Paul says that when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman: the promises from Isaiah and Micah came true right on time. Jesus came to redeem us, which means to buy us back, so we could be adopted into God's family. Then God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, so we can call God "Abba, Father," a close family word like "Dad." This week we saw God promise a child (Isaiah 9:6), a great light (Isaiah 9:2), and a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and we learned that God never breaks a promise and is never late. Because of Jesus, we are not slaves but God's own children.
dailies.enochActivity: Snuggle up with a parent and say, "God is my Father, and I am his child!" Then shout, "Jesus came, just like God promised!"
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 6, what does the Spirit call out? Why is it special that we can call God that?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: "Abba, Father" (verse 6). It's special because it means we are God's own children, close to him like kids with a loving dad (verse 7).
dailies.jordyn2: Verses 4–6 show the Father sending his Son and then sending the Spirit of his Son. How does that connect to what we learned about one God in three persons? What does it mean for you to be God's "heir" (verse 7)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The Father sent the Son to redeem us and sent the Spirit into our hearts, so all three persons work together to save us (verses 4–6). An heir receives what belongs to the family; God's children will share in everything he has for them, forever (verse 7).
dailies.passageText: 4 But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship. 6 Because you are his sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who calls out, “Abba, Father.” 7 So you are no longer a slave, but God’s child; and since you are his child, God has made you also an heir.
